ai.definition: Thermal/Molten-Salt Storage is a method of energy storage where thermal energy is captured by heating molten salt and stored for later use. The heated salt can be used to generate power through steam turbines or provide process heat directly.
ai.howItWorks: Nitrate salts, which are inexpensive and have high thermal capacity, are heated to very high temperatures (typically around 500°C) in a thermal storage system. This heated salt is then stored in insulated tanks until needed. When required, the hot salt is passed through a heat exchanger where it transfers its thermal energy to water, producing steam that drives a turbine to generate electricity or directly provides process heat.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the intermittency issues of solar power and other renewable sources by storing excess thermal energy during peak production times for use when generation is low. This makes solar power more dispatchable and reliable.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves sourcing and refining nitrate salts, constructing insulated storage tanks, and setting up heat exchangers and steam turbines or direct heating systems.
ai.buildProcess: Construction begins with site preparation, followed by the installation of thermal storage tanks, heat transfer systems, and power generation components. The system is then commissioned for testing before full operation can commence.
ai.costDrivers: Costs are driven primarily by material prices (salts), insulation quality, and the efficiency of heat exchangers. Construction costs also play a significant role due to the need for robust thermal storage tanks and high-temperature components.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in early commercial stages with some pilot projects and limited deployments, but it has strong potential for wider adoption as renewable energy systems continue to grow.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by region. In regions where renewable energy targets are set, there may be incentives or mandates that encourage the use of storage technologies like thermal/molten-salt storage.
ai.risks: Technical risks include ensuring long-term stability and safety of high-temperature systems, managing corrosion issues in salt tanks, and maintaining insulation integrity over time. Economic risks involve fluctuating material costs and competition from other energy storage solutions.
ai.profitability: Profitability depends on the specific application. In regions with strong solar resources and supportive policies, thermal/molten-salt storage can be economically viable for both CSP dispatch and industrial heat applications.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development could focus on improving cycle efficiency, reducing material costs, and enhancing system integration with other renewable energy technologies to increase overall energy system reliability and cost-effectiveness.

glossary.def: A method of storing heat for later use, often used in conjunction with solar thermal power plants or industrial processes.
A form of solar power generation that uses mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a small area to produce high temperatures and generate electricity.
The ability of an energy source to provide power on demand, as opposed to being dependent on the time of day or weather conditions.

subsystems.name: Hot and cold salt tanks
subsystems.role: hold the same nitrate salt at two temperatures — roughly 290 °C and 565 °C — and so store the energy.

subsystems.name: Solar or heat source
parts: heliostat field and central receiver, or parabolic-trough collectors
electric immersion heaters or heat pumps (power-to-heat variants)

subsystems.name: Charging loop
subsystems.role: moves cold salt up to the hot tank.

subsystems.name: Discharging loop
subsystems.role: taps hot salt to make steam or hot gas.
parts: steam generator or process heat exchanger

subsystems.name: Steam cycle and generator
subsystems.role: turns the delivered heat into electricity where power is the product.

subsystems.name: Freeze protection and controls
subsystems.role: keeps salt above its freezing point, around 220 °C, everywhere in the loop.

buildSteps.title: Fix the duty
buildSteps.detail: Decide the temperature range, hours of discharge and whether the output is electricity, steam or direct process heat — this sets the salt volume and tank size.

buildSteps.title: Select the salt
buildSteps.detail: Most plants use a 60/40 sodium-nitrate/potassium-nitrate mix, which is cheap and stable to about 565 °C; chloride or carbonate salts are studied for hotter operation.

buildSteps.title: Build the tanks
buildSteps.detail: Large insulated steel tanks are erected on engineered foundations, with internal distributors so incoming salt does not mix the hot and cold layers.

buildSteps.title: Build the collector or heater
buildSteps.detail: A heliostat field and tower, a trough field, or banks of electric heaters are installed to deliver heat into the loop.

buildSteps.title: Install the molten-salt loop
buildSteps.detail: Pumps, valves, expansion vessels and heat exchangers are fitted, and the whole circuit is wrapped in trace heating and insulation.

buildSteps.title: Melt and fill
buildSteps.detail: Salt arrives as solid pellets or flakes; it is melted with auxiliary heaters and circulated to fill the tanks, a slow first-time process.

buildSteps.title: Charge
buildSteps.detail: The heat source raises cold salt to the hot tank, storing energy for hours at a time.

buildSteps.title: Discharge and deliver
buildSteps.detail: Hot salt is pumped through a steam generator or process exchanger, returns to the cold tank, and the steam drives a turbine or feeds an industrial plant.

buildSteps.title: Operate with freeze watch
buildSteps.detail: Controls hold every pipe above the salt's freezing point, since a solid plug can shut down the plant.

prerequisites.tech: Concentrating solar collectors or large electric heaters
prerequisites.why: they supply the heat that charges the store.
decades of use in solar thermal plants have proven pumps, valves and materials.
salt must circulate hundreds of times a day without leaking or seizing.
electric thermal storage only pays when power is very cheap for part of the day.
many factories need continuous steam or heat that a store must match exactly.

pathway.milestone: concentrating solar plants with 8–15 hours of molten-salt storage, such as Gemasolar and Noor Ouarzazate
pathway.unlocks: solar power delivered into the evening and night.

pathway.milestone: electric thermal stores using salt, sand or brick feeding industrial steam and heat
pathway.unlocks: decarbonising factories that cannot run on intermittent power directly.

pathway.milestone: retiring coal plants rebuilt around thermal stores and electric heaters
pathway.unlocks: reuse of existing turbines, grid connections and sites.

pathway.milestone: multi-day thermal storage paired with very cheap wind and solar
pathway.unlocks: firm, dispatchable heat and power over week-long lulls.
